summary: Port reproduces the original's per-pixel autumn-ember twinkle — same instant ignition, same exponential decay rate, same density and spatial randomness — but its palette hues sit noticeably more orange/amber than the original's deep reds, and it never reproduces the original's periodic ~33 s total freeze.
observations: Both sides are alive on the default rig (strip, 60 px), no compile or runtime errors, and neither binds sensors (wantsSensors false on both, sensors 'off').
Both sides expose ZERO controls (probe: 'no settable controls' on orig and port), so there are no dials to compare and no control-surface mismatch.

Mechanism matches exactly. --dump of 30 consecutive 0.1 s frames (label 'envelope', t=30.0-32.9 s) shows both sides doing the same thing per pixel: a pixel ignites instantly to a random peak (orig peaks seen 128/148/181/204/222; port 127/136/205/232), holds one fixed hue, then decays exponentially to 0 and stays dark for a few hundred ms before re-igniting with a new hue. Decay ratio per 0.1 s is ~0.952 on the original (222 -> 212 -> 203 -> 194) and ~0.957 on the port (232 -> 222 -> 213 -> 204) — effectively identical.
Ignition rate matches: ~0.3-0.4 re-ignitions per pixel per second on both, counted over the same 3 s window and 8 pixels (orig 9 ignitions, port 8).

Spatial character matches: pixels are statistically independent on both sides (spatial autocorrelation of per-pixel brightness at lags 1-4 is orig -0.07/-0.05/0.03/-0.04, port -0.02/-0.03/-0.01/-0.05 across 18 sampled frames). No travelling features, no slopes in either waterfall.
Lit density matches: over 18 frames x 60 px, pixels above max-channel 40 are orig 403/1080 (37%) vs port 377/1080 (35%).
Both palettes are fully saturated (saturation 1.00 at every quantile on both) and contain NO blue at all (meanB min=max=0 on both, in every run).

PALETTE HUE SHIFT. Both sides draw from a small discrete hue set, but the port's is stretched warmer. Bright-pixel hue histogram over 18 frames spanning t=20-73 s: orig 0 deg (123), 10.7 deg (114), 21.4 deg (158), rare 39.6 deg (8); port 0 deg (113), 12.4 deg (125), 26.9 deg (135), rare 46.5 deg (4). Same count of palette entries and same rough spacing pattern, each entry pushed ~15-25% further round toward orange/yellow.

Consequence in the aggregate stats: the port runs consistently greener. meanG avg orig 8.5 vs port 10.7 at 20 fps / 60 s; 8.2 vs 11.0 at baseline; 8.5 vs 10.8 on seed 7. meanR is essentially equal (41.9 vs 42.1). Visually the original reads as embers/deep red with orange flecks, the port as orange/amber with red flecks.

ORIGINAL FREEZES PERIODICALLY, PORT NEVER DOES. At 20 fps the original's whole strip goes completely static for 32.8 s starting at t=81.8, 196.4, 311.1 and 425.8 s — a dead-exact 114.65 s period, 28.6% duty. Verified as a true freeze, not a quantization false-read: a --dump at t=85, 90, 95 and 104 s is byte-identical on the original (mean abs diff 0.00 across a 19 s span) while the port over the same times differs by 21-24 mean abs. The port shows zero freeze frames over the whole 0-480 s timeline (0 zero-motion frames in 4800 at 20 fps for t=240-480).

The frozen phase looks like a normal mid-decay snapshot of the pattern held still (see freeze-dump/orig.png: clean vertical stripes, no fade, no black-out), so during it the original is a static striped picture while the port keeps twinkling.

The freeze's numbers smell like a clock artefact rather than intent: duration is 32.768 s exactly (= 65.536/2, i.e. a whole Pixelblaze time() unit) and the period is 114.65 s = 1.75 x 65.536 s. Its onset time also moves with fps (t=34.5 s at 2 fps, 38.4 at 5, 46.7 at 10, 81.8 at 20), which a deliberate design would not do.

Because the original spends ~29% of its time frozen, coarse-window motion averages understate it and look like a port speed error that is not there: survey (60 s, 5 fps) motion avg orig 3.3 vs port 5.4, but 3.3 / (1 - 0.36 frozen) = 5.2, and in a clean active window the two agree (baseline 20 fps: orig 1.4, port 1.5; t=40-60 s at 20 fps: orig 1.4, port 1.5).

Neither side is frame-rate-coupled in the same way as the other, and both are time-based: motion avg falls with fps on both (orig 6.9/3.3/2.0/1.4/0.4 and port 12.6/5.4/2.7/1.5/0.8 at 2/5/10/20/40 fps) and the decorrelation curve is fps-independent. Decorrelation timescale matches: mean abs diff vs t0 rises to a plateau of ~20-24 by lag 1-2 s on BOTH sides (orig 1.7/5.6/10.8/17.3/24.0 at lags 0.05/0.2/0.5/1.0/2.0 s; port 1.1/4.4/10.3/20.0/23.6).
Seed independence checked: at --seed 7 the same picture holds (orig meanG 8.5 vs port 10.8, motion 1.4 vs 1.5, both brightnessTrend steady), so none of the above is a one-seed fluke.
Neither side drifts or dies: brightnessTrend 'steady' on both in every 20 fps run, including the t=240-480 s window.
feedback: Palette hue is the one clearly actionable gap. The original's spark hues cluster at 0, ~10.7, ~21.4 degrees (with a rare ~39.6 deg amber); the port's cluster at 0, ~12.4, ~26.9 degrees (rare ~46.5 deg). Pull the port's non-red palette entries back toward red by roughly 15-25% of their hue angle so the strip reads as deep-red embers with orange flecks rather than orange with red flecks. Target aggregate: meanG ~8.5 against meanR ~42 on a 60 s / 20 fps strip run (the port currently posts meanG ~10.7 at the same meanR).

Everything else about the spark model is already right and should NOT be touched: instant ignition to a random peak up to ~230, fixed hue held for the whole decay, exponential decay of ~0.95 per 0.1 s (about a 2 s visible lifetime), ~0.35 re-ignitions per pixel per second, independent pixels, fully saturated, zero blue.

The original's 32.8 s total freeze every 114.65 s is the other divergence, but investigate before replicating it. The exact 32.768 s duration, the 65.536 s-multiple period, and the fps-dependent onset all point at a time() wrap / accumulator artefact in the original rather than an intended 'still' phase, and a viewer would read it as the strip hanging. If it turns out to be intentional, the port needs a phase where every pixel stops mid-decay and holds its exact colour for ~33 s before resuming; if it is an artefact, leave the port's continuous twinkle as-is and record the difference.
No control work is needed: the original exposes no controls, so the port correctly exposes none.
